newsitem.title: UK: Blair won't ask Chirac for EMU delay - UK officials.
newsitem.headline: Blair won't ask Chirac for EMU delay - UK officials.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair, well aware of the political capital that Paris and Bonn have staked on Europe's single currency, has no intention of trying to persuade French President Jacques Chirac to delay the project, British officials said on Wednesday.
Blair will hold talks with Chirac in Paris on Wednesday evening as part of a round of diplomacy ahead of next week's European Union summit in Amsterdam.

The summit will aim to conclude a new treaty overhauling the EU's rules and institutions, but it is likely to be overshadowed by doubts as to whether the single currency can proceed on schedule in 1999.

Aides said Blair would stress the need to avoid fudging the eligibility criteria for the single currency but believes it would be wrong and counterproductive to take a hostile stance given strong Franco-German determination that it should succeed.
"He's not going to rain on their parade," a senior aide said.
Blair has said it is very unlikely that Britain will be among the first wave of countries to sign up for economic and monetary union (EMU).

But the prime minister believes Britain is well placed to influence the project because it has not ruled out joining later. "The option is genuinely open that we will join at some stage," the aide said.
He said Blair believes Britain would lose its influence if, like the previous Conservative government, it was seen to be trying to wreck EMU.

Prospects for EMU have been thrown into turmoil by a row in Germany over plans to revalue gold reserves to help meet EMU targets and by the new French socialist government's demand for more time to consider the stability pact that will underpin budgetary discipline in the new single currency zone.
As well as discussing EMU, Blair and Chirac will go over the obstacles still in the way of a new EU treaty in Amsterdam.
On the British side, the trickiest problem is its demand -- shared by Ireland -- to retain control over its borders.
Blair spoke by telephone on Wednesday morning with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, who holds the rotating EU presidency, but failed to resolve the problem, British officials said.
London's fierce opposition to the Franco-German apsiration to integrate the Western European Union, an informal defence alliance, into the EU is another big sticking point, they said.
